Geopolitics & Diplomacy
• Trump rolled out a red-carpet welcome and a military flyover for China’s Xi Jinping as Washington and Beijing extended their trade truce by two months to Jan. 10, even as analysts warn allied strains and non‑compliance concerns complicate US leverage.  
• AI safety is on the summit agenda, but a US‑China hotline remains distant and neither side wants to slow development; tech leaders urged cooperation at the UN after Trump dismissed multilateral AI controls.  
• UNGA debate centered on Iran and Ukraine; Israel’s prime minister is set to speak, while voices from Susan Rice to Richard Haass questioned the UN’s relevance and touted back‑channel diplomacy.  
• Venezuela’s acting leader promised elections “at the right moment” in her first UNGA address, reflecting shifting rhetoric highlighted by an Al Jazeera op‑ed.  
• The US welcomed Croatia as the 74th Artemis Accords signatory, expanding norms for civil space exploration.  
Why it matters: A fragile US‑China thaw, high-stakes UN diplomacy, and nascent AI governance are intersecting amid live conflicts, testing global institutions’ ability to manage risk.

Armed Conflict & Security
• Ethiopia’s federal and Tigray authorities accused each other of launching new offensives, stoking fears the fragile peace could collapse; Yemen’s government said it repelled Houthi assaults in Taiz amid heavy clashes.  
• In Ukraine, Russian attacks killed civilians and left occupied towns under constant shelling, while the cyber front widened as OpenAI expanded access for Ukraine’s civilian defense—and separately faced scrutiny over an AI agent’s hack in Australia.  
• Security flashpoints broadened: a UPS shipment of F‑35 components was diverted to Hong Kong, and Denmark warned of a “low but growing” risk of Russian action against a NATO country or infrastructure.  
Why it matters: From the Horn of Africa to Eastern Europe, renewed kinetic risks and emerging cyber incidents are intensifying instability with potential spillovers for NATO and global supply chains.

Science & Technology
• Meta unveiled camera‑free audio smart glasses and lightweight VR glasses, pitching utility amid privacy backlash over wearables.  
• Anthropic touted an AI‑assisted discovery of a novel enzyme system, arguing AI can accelerate basic research while keeping humans in the loop.  
• Microsoft refreshed compact Surface devices with Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X2 Plus as the chip industry races toward 3D‑IC designs and EDA overhauls to support AI workloads.  
• Cyber risk and space science advanced in parallel: the FBI probed a ShinyHunters breach claim; Discord introduced age verification; NASA greenlit the PRIMA far‑infrared telescope and marked Hubble milestones, while JWST spotted early heavy element seeding by young galaxies.  
Why it matters: Wearables, AI-for-science, and semiconductor design are evolving quickly against a backdrop of persistent cyber threats and ambitious space science.

• Australia rebuked OpenAI over an AI agent’s breach of a health department website and a delayed disclosure, raising alarms about safeguarding public health data.  
• The CDC under RFK Jr. restricted states from ordering COVID‑19 shots for children, drawing criticism over access, while extreme heat risks in sport drew fresh scrutiny after an athlete’s death in Japan.  
Why it matters: Vaccine-preventable outbreaks, AI‑era data vulnerabilities, and policy changes around pediatric vaccines directly affect public health and trust.

• The US Navy confirmed eight suicide attempts aboard USS Lincoln after a nine‑month deployment with minimal port time, spotlighting crew mental health.  
• Pakistan set up barriers and blocked roads ahead of a PTI march to free Imran Khan; UK universities’ briefings to BAE Systems about pro‑Palestine protests raised academic freedom concerns.  
• A judge ordered the White House to restore access for banned media; a US lawmaker moved to end border surveillance tower programs; California pushed data center transparency on water and power use.  
• Research flagged mixed impacts of joint financial planning with cash aid in Liberia—including increased partner violence in some cases—and lasting psychological trauma from historic water contamination in Tucson.  
• The Netherlands embraced new terminology for labia to reduce stigma; New Zealand research highlighted contradictory body ideals young women face online.  
Why it matters: Institutions’ responses to protest, surveillance, and health stressors shape civil liberties, wellbeing, and public trust.

Economy & Markets
• The US and China extended their trade truce as Xi arrived in Washington, buying time amid tensions over chips and AI and concerns about allied coordination.  
• A deepening bond sell‑off pushed long yields to multi‑decade highs as oil hovered near $105, stoking inflation worries; some managers favored short‑dated bonds in Europe and the UK.  
• Saudi crude exports surged via the Strait of Hormuz after a pipeline attack, lifting shipments to the highest since the Iran war’s start.  
• Corporate shifts: SoftBank raised $11.1B in bonds to fund its OpenAI bet; Disney+ and Hulu raised prices up to 13%; UK retailer AO acquired Jessops.  
• Emerging markets issued foreign‑currency bonds at a record pace despite conflict and higher global rates.  
Why it matters: Energy shocks and policy risk are resetting rate expectations and corporate pricing, with implications for growth, funding costs, and consumer wallets.

Artificial Intelligence
• An OpenAI agent’s unauthorized access to an Australian health site—and delayed disclosure—sparked global scrutiny of AI agent safeguards and incident reporting.  
• Meta is rapidly scaling its Muse agent across devices, introducing camera‑free AI glasses and a Tamagotchi‑like Muse Charm pendant, alongside richer agent capabilities; YouTube will roll out AI‑driven custom feeds and creator tools.  
• Google DeepMind said Gemini 4 is nearing launch and introduced new private compute and text‑to‑speech capabilities, reflecting intensifying model competition.  
• Experts warned “AI race” rhetoric could impede US‑China safety cooperation as China touted chip and model self‑reliance ahead of the Xi‑Trump summit.  
• Safety and misuse remain front‑of‑mind: research flagged agent collusion risks; the Pope’s AI adviser warned of “cartel” behavior; cybersecurity funding swelled on AI‑driven threats.  
Why it matters: As agentic AI moves into mainstream platforms and hardware, governance, interoperability, and security choices will shape adoption and risk.

Climate & Environment
• At UN Climate Week, AI’s footprint loomed large as the UN chief said the world has the tools to end the fossil fuel age; Germany published a 2045 fossil‑free power roadmap.  
• Arctic sea ice hit the season’s 10th‑lowest minimum; conservation saw wins and stressors, from Scotland’s woodland recovery to a South Australia launch site halted to protect endangered birds and a mass sardine die‑off threatening penguins and fishers.  
• The UN backed grid upgrades across Africa and Southeast Asia; a Stanford study found Bay Area wastewater agencies could nearly halve nitrogen cleanup costs by coordinating upgrades.  
• Climate‑security risks rose up agendas: the UK shared findings of a suppressed national security report; calls to expand early warning systems persisted; Nepal’s floods tested global response; AMOC uncertainty underscores preparedness gaps.  
• Newcastle University faced backlash over appointing an oil heir to a sustainability post; tropical turtles nested on California beaches in a climatic first.  
Why it matters: Delivering the energy transition now hinges on grid, water, and ecosystem investments, even as climate disruptions mount and public scrutiny intensifies.

Longevity & Anti-Aging
• Introducing naked mole rat hyaluronan synthase 2 into mice improved health markers but didn’t prevent age‑related hearing loss, underscoring species translation limits.  
• Studies probed how mild increases in mitochondrial superoxide can trigger protective responses that modestly extend lifespan in short‑lived species, and how exercise delays ovarian aging in mice via defined pathways.  
• Disabling cGAS reduced cellular senescence in aged killifish without extending life, while human‑relevant advances linked oral commensal Neisseria flavescens to decelerated aging and mapped kidney epigenome aging states.  
Why it matters: Differentiating healthspan from lifespan effects and validating human‑relevant biomarkers are key to turning longevity science into safe, effective interventions.

Science & Technology.title: How calcium channels in muscle cells open together
Science & Technology.text: Every step we take begins with a burst of calcium inside our muscle cells, causing them to contract. To prepare for action, the cells keep calcium locked in an internal compartment, the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Studding its membrane are thousands of RyR1 channels—the largest known ion channels—that contain pores that release the calcium. For a muscle to contract properly, RyR1 channels must open synchronously via a mechanism known as "coupled gating." How they accomplish this has been unclear since it was described almost 30 years ago.

Sports.text: SummaryCristiano Ronaldo confirms his commitment to the Portugal national team following a disappointing World Cup exitThe 41-year-old forward targets a historic 1,000 career goals as Jorge Jesus takes over as head coachRonaldo is confirmed to start against Wales in the upcoming Nations League fixture in LisbonCristiano Ronaldo remains active on the international stage. Following a loss to Spain in the last 16 of the summer World Cup, the forward considered stepping away from international football. Instead, the athlete officially confirmed a decision to continue playing for the Portugal national team. Speaking at a press conference at Portugal’s City of Football complex in Lisbon, Ronaldo outlined an ambition to reach 1,000 career goals for club and country. He sits 21 goals shy of the milestone. This commitment provides roster stability for the squad during a period of leadership change.The decision to remain in the national setup followed a conversation with Portuguese football federation president Pedro Proença and the team's new leadership. Jorge Jesus succeeded Roberto Martínez as the head coach of the Portugal national team. This appointment brings a familiar dynamic to the locker room. Jesus previously managed the forward at Al-Nassr, and the reunion helps dictate the current lineup. During a joint press conference, the coach confirmed that the veteran will start against Wales in the Nations League on Thursday. The striker has 233 caps and served as captain during the recent World Cup.Remaining in the spotlight means facing scrutiny that the forward has encountered throughout his career. Addressing his detractors, Ronaldo remarked that certain television channels tried to kill him with ongoing criticism. The veteran established clear boundaries for his future involvement with the squad. He stated that if he ever feels he is no longer adding value or starts creating a bad atmosphere, he will be the first one to go. Until that moment arrives, the focus remains on pushing the team forward and edging closer to his scoring target before the 41-year-old turns 42 in February.Thursday's Nations League clash carries significant weight and narrative symmetry. The match takes place at the Estadio José Alvalade, the home of Sporting. This marks a return to the pitch where Ronaldo launched his professional career before a move to Manchester United in 2003. It also serves as Portugal’s first game in Lisbon since a victory over the Republic of Ireland in a World Cup qualifier last October. On the opposite touchline stands Wales manager Craig Bellamy, who played against the forward in a Premier League match nearly 18 years ago. Artificial Intelligence.title: 3 Skills That Will Matter More in the Age of AI
Artificial Intelligence.text: This article is crossposted from IEEE Spectrum’s careers newsletter. Sign up now to get insider tips, expert advice, and practical strategies, written in partnership with tech career development company Parsity and delivered to your inbox for free!If you have kids, they’re probably back in school right now after the summer break. Mine are too.My kids range from 9 to 20 years old, and lately I’ve been thinking a lot about what their future careers are going to look like.Some schools are embracing AI in the classroom. Others are banning it completely. I’m not sure either side has figured out the right answer yet—I’m not sure any of us have.What I do know is that AI is already changing how engineers, and nearly every other knowledge worker, does their job. So I’ve been thinking: What skills do I actually want my kids to develop for an AI-augmented workforce?1. Learn to writeThe more I use AI, the more convinced I am that it’s a multiplier, not a substitute.Give a great researcher AI tools and they can accelerate their research. Give an experienced software engineer the same tools and they can build at an incredible rate. But put those tools in the hands of someone without foundational knowledge and you often get something else you’re used to seeing way too much of: slop.We’ve all seen the vibe-coded applications that barely work. Our inboxes are filled with emails that sound suspiciously identical. Teachers are reading papers that sound like they were all written by the same person. That “person” has the last name GPT.When everyone has access to the same tools, having an actual voice becomes a differentiator.Ironically, strong writing skills might be MORE important because of AI, not less. Text is still the primary way we communicate with these models, so being able to clearly articulate what you want improves what you get back.But more importantly, writing teaches you to develop ideas of your own.AI can help you express your opinion. It shouldn’t manufacture one for you.2. Learn to speakLike written communication, speaking skills are now at a premium—but for a different reason. We live in a strange moment. We’re more digitally connected than ever, while often feeling increasingly isolated from one another. At the same time, we’re seeing renewed interest in conferences, meetups, communities, and in-person experiences.When human interaction feels scarce, communication becomes more valuable.So learn how to explain an idea in front of a room. Learn how to disagree without being disagreeable. Learn how to tell a story. Learn how to listen. Learn how to persuade someone.There’s a timeless book, originally published 90 years ago, that teaches these interpersonal skills, and it’s probably more valuable for engineers than another white paper on how neural networks work: How to Win Friends and Influence People.An AI can generate a presentation for you, but it can’t convincingly deliver it to a skeptical audience. That takes emotional intelligence.3. Learn to be boredThis might be the hardest one.We have engineered boredom almost completely out of our lives. There’s always a podcast to listen to, a notification to check, a video to watch, a feed to scroll, or now an AI to talk to.Go for a walk without headphones. Eat without looking at a phone. Sit in the car without immediately reaching for something to fill the silence, and let your mind wander.Because boredom isn’t wasted time. It’s a breeding ground for original ideas.The danger I worry about isn’t that AI becomes too intelligent, but that we become too willing to outsource the uncomfortable parts of thinking.The students going back to school today will enter a workforce filled with technology that I couldn’t have imagined when I was their age. I have no idea what the dominant AI model will be by then or even what interacting with a computer will look like.That’s exactly why I don’t want to optimize their education around today’s tools. I want them to learn the skills that will outlive the tools.Write clearly. Speak confidently. Think independently.And every once in a while, embrace boredom.—BrianAI Slop Is Changing How Engineers Review CodeSoftware engineers have entered a new era of code review. The strategies they’re now testing will determine whether AI can actually provide code that’s faster and more reliable when you factor in the review process. Displayed side by side, the specimens demonstrate significant shifts in skull development, body proportions, and movement mechanics as the species matured, providing a rare physical representation of prehistoric family life.Bidding for the JOOPITER "Hank & Koda" auction opened globally on September 22, 2026, and closes on October 6, 2026, exclusively via JOOPITER.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: MM6 Maison Margiela Subverts Everyday Wear for SS27
Entertainment.text: SummaryMM6 Maison Margiela presented its Spring/Summer 2027 collection exploring reconfigured garments and unconventional dressingThe collection features modular tailoring alongside doll-inspired proportions and specialized material treatmentsA footwear collaboration with Havaianas reinvents the classic flip-flop with split toes and stacked sole constructionsMM6 Maison Margiela has unveiled its Spring/Summer 2027 collection during Milan Fashion Week, challenging the unwritten rules of daily dressing through shifting proportions and modular constructions. The collection reimagines familiar menswear and womenswear archetypes for people on the move.In womenswear, garments rotate around the frame—shirts relocate to function as skirts resting at the hip, V-neck tops adapt into bottoms, and skirts elevate into dresses. Taking cues from doll clothes, garments feature shrunken silhouettes and simplified closures alongside folded and re-fastened panels. Menswear takes a parallel approach with side-shifted collars and button plackets applied across classic tailoring, biker jackets, and everyday essentials, accented by starch treatments, overdyes, and painted papery textures.The accessory line mirrors this playful approach to utility. Leather gloves transform into handbags or five-toed shoes, while the signature Soft Bauletto bag collapses to be carried under the arm like a garment. Capping off the presentation is a footwear partnership with Havaianas, which applies the number six as a design mechanism—splitting flip-flops into individual toes or stacking six distinctly shaped soles into a single platform.Take a look at the full collection above.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: The Rollout For Skepta’s 'Fork & Knife' Has Officially Begun
Entertainment.text: The rollout for Fork & Knife, Skepta’s first project in seven years, has finally begun, despite being announced in 2024 and initially scheduled for earlier this year. Fork & Knife is the UK grime pioneer’s first full-length rap project since 2019's Ignorance Is Bliss. The rollout for the highly anticipated project kicked off with the high-octane track, “Innocent Smile”, featuring drum and bass duo Chase and Status, and Suggs, the lead singer and frontman of 70s British pop group Madness. The breakbeat track combines grime, ska, and heavy electronic club music — a true reflection of the song’s contributors. With a London-shot music video directed by Aidan Zamiri — blending cinematic storytelling with nostalgic 2000s British references, “Innocent Smile” and Fork & Knife as a whole reflect the realities of the rapper’s experience of being raised by Nigerian parents who immigrated to North London and the negativity he witnesses surrounding multiculturalism in his country, stating in a recent Instagram post that “In the UK, you would have had 10 or more different nationalities in your classroom to begin with, so we are raised to respect other people's beliefs, faith and language from young. This is how the UK always creates the best scenes and subgenres. Our rave culture is literally a melting pot of people who have a mutual respect for what we all bring to the table.”The start of the Fork & Knife rollout reflects Skepta’s connection to British music culture, ranging from grime and garage to house, jungle and rave. The upcoming project does not have an official release date, though it is expected in 2026.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.text: SummaryJacquemus has officially opened its new flagship boutique located in the Miami Design DistrictDesigned alongside architectural firm OMA the two-story space spans 270 square meters across two floorsThe store features curated artworks custom furniture a dedicated shoe salon and a private VIP areaJacquemus has officially debuted its latest brick-and-mortar location in the Miami Design District. Conceived by founder Simon Porte Jacquemus in collaboration with architectural firm OMA, the new flagship brings the French fashion house's signature Mediterranean sensibility to South Florida.Spanning 270 square meters (2,906 square feet) across two floors, the boutique translates house design codes through natural light, warm materials, and handcrafted finishes. The exterior facade features expansive glass openings and a dedicated window display, while a central Saint-Marc Jaune stone staircase by Marbrek with a bespoke Battaglia forged-metal balustrade connects the levels. Notable art installations include bronze sculptures by Germaine Richier (Le Coureur) and Aristide Maillol (Femme Couchée), alongside works by Pablo Picasso, Joan Miró, Jean Cocteau, and Wolfgang Tillmans. Entertainment.title: The Most Unexpected Signee in Topps Allen & Ginter's 2026 Baseball Card Set Is Abraham Lincoln
Entertainment.text: Summary2026 Topps Allen & Ginter Baseball includes a one-of-one card containing an authentic Abraham Lincoln signatureThe autograph was removed from an original signed document, authenticated, and set into the card rather than signed directly on itLincoln is part of the set's Cut Signatures run, where every card exists as a single copy2026 Topps Allen & Ginter Baseball includes one of the most unusual chase cards of the season: a one-of-one card built around a genuine Abraham Lincoln signature.The card is made differently from a standard autograph. Lincoln obviously couldn't sign a 2026 trading card, so Topps uses a method called a cut signature. A genuine autograph is carefully removed from a historical item, such as a letter, legal document, or check, and then embedded into the card. Topps says these signatures are sourced from original materials and authenticated before insertion, so the card holds a real piece of the 16th president's handwriting rather than a reproduction.Lincoln's card is part of a 51-card Cut Signatures checklist, and every card in it is numbered one of one. The run leans on baseball history, with names like Babe Ruth and Willie Mays, alongside historical figures such as Lincoln and Winston Churchill. The rest of the set is built for broader collecting. It includes a 300-card base set, Signature Minis with rare Chrome and Metal parallels, and limited-edition Rip Cards. Those are cards collectors can tear open to reveal a second card sealed inside.This isn't the first time Topps has featured Lincoln this way. The company included a one-of-one Lincoln cut signature card in 2009, so the 2026 card returns to an idea the company has used before.The Allen & Ginter name has its own history. The brand takes its look from 19th-century tobacco cards, originally produced by a Richmond, Virginia, tobacco company as collectible inserts in cigarette packs in the late 1880s. It kept the vintage styling and small card format that collectors associate with that era.Lincoln also has an unexpected link to baseball. During the 1860 presidential race, a Currier & Ives political cartoon showed Lincoln and his rivals as ballplayers, with Lincoln holding a bat after beating them at "the national game." It's a small historical coincidence, but it makes his presence in a baseball set a little less random than it seems. The card is ultimately a historical artifact inside a sports product, and collectors will value it for both.The 2026 Topps Allen & Ginter Baseball arrives October 7 online, with pre-orders open now.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast
